Text | Zhuoyi Ma

Editors | Fanyu Meng, Er Mu

“I don’t have the patience to read the whole thing, just give me the bottom line”:

1. Any sound can be evaluated on three levels, the physical, the perceptual and the cognitive, and within each level you can build suitable dimensions or angles of evaluation.

2. No level is better or worse than another; each is simply more or less suited to the job.

3. When you talk about sound with someone, make sure you are both on the same level. No “interplanetary communication.”

Best read when you have time to kill, because the writing style is extremely laid-back.

When it comes to judging sound, you may know first-hand what it feels like to question someone else’s taste, or to have your own taste questioned. If you are a mixing engineer or an acoustic engineer, you may sneer at all that mystical, woo-woo vocabulary. If you are a sound performer or creator, you may think the underlying theory and technology are nothing but a pile of cold numbers and dull, abstract code. Then the two sides have to work together. You stick to your guns, I stick to mine, each convinced the other is an idiot and that only they have seen the truth about sound. It ends either in a falling-out or in grudging compromises that torture everyone, and the result is a steaming pile of garbage…

Please, let’s not talk past each other like a nerdy programmer and a clueless product manager! In reality, though, some talking past each other is unavoidable. Each side’s education and line of work all but guarantee that their ideas about “judging sound” will never overlap perfectly. So each side judges from inside its own field, through its own fixed lens, in terms that make sense to it.

So here’s the question: is there really no universal, best-of-both-worlds, everybody-wins way of judging sound?

No, there really isn’t.

Think I’m just being cheeky? Hold on. As the saying goes, give someone a fish and you feed them for a day; teach them to fish and you feed them for a lifetime. A perfect perspective or standard that satisfies everyone’s needs really doesn’t exist. But acoustics does have a universal, scientific methodology, suitable for all ages, for building evaluation criteria. It isn’t the fish itself, but as a way of fishing it is thoroughly reliable and fair. That is what I want to talk about today.

“Methodology” sounds grand, but put simply it is just a way of thinking, one with a system to it. So below I’ll share what that way of thinking is and how to put it to use in daily life and at work.

Before the methodology itself, we need one concept: the three levels of evaluating sound.

In the field of sound, evaluating a sound is usually divided into three levels: physical, perceptual and cognitive. You can also think of them as three stages of evaluation. Sound engineers, for example, tend to evaluate at the physical level, ear doctors at the perceptual level, and sound artists at the cognitive level.

Sounds a bit convoluted? Let me break each level down, piece by piece.

The physical level

The physical level is all about describing the world objectively. Things are what they are: it is completely impartial and does not bend to human will. For example, the sound pressure level of some sound at some position is 30 dB; 3.14 seconds into the recording, the energy in the 2000–2050 Hz band is such-and-such. These cold numbers are perfectly impartial. They don’t fudge or fake anything; they record the sound exactly as it truly is. That is the impartial part. Or take this: 200 million years ago a meteorite struck the Earth. It doesn’t take a genius to know it must have made an enormous bang. But can we say, “There were no humans 200 million years ago, so nobody heard it, so the sound didn’t exist”? Absurd, right? That example shows the “independent of human will” part.

So evaluation at the physical level is objective, complete and neutral. Notice anything interesting? That’s right: evaluating at the physical level is really just recording and measuring sound.

Dimensions at the physical level include frequency, sound pressure level, time, signal-to-noise ratio and so on.

The perceptual level

The perceptual level is about how people perceive sound, that is, what a sound physically feels like to hear. When something is too loud, for instance, your ears hurt, because the body has a built-in warning system for sounds that are too loud. That raises a question: isn’t the sound we hear simply the real sound out in the world? Not really. The simplest example is ultrasound and infrasound. Our ears cannot perceive them at all, yet they truly exist; the human auditory system just can’t pick them up, while other animals can. Bats hear ultrasound, and elephants can sense infrasound. Another example: the “loudness” we talk about at work doesn’t necessarily match the actual sound energy out in the world, which is why we have equal-loudness contours (sounds at the same sound pressure level but different frequencies are perceived as differently loud). The ear is far less sensitive at low frequencies than in the 1–3 kHz range, for instance. That also explains why a burly bass, even with more air in his lungs, really doesn’t carry as well as a slight soprano.

The gap between “the sound we perceive” and “the sound that actually happens in the world” ultimately comes down to traits that living things have acquired over a long evolution. One explanation for why humans are so sensitive in the 1–3 kHz range is that this is where the cries of baby mammals are concentrated, which helped our ancestors raise their young and hunt.

Dimensions at the perceptual level include loudness, tonality, sharpness, spatiality (judging where a sound comes from and how big the room is) and so on.

The cognitive level

The cognitive level offers a great deal of freedom, mainly because evaluation here runs through each person’s own understanding. And even though we all come with “two arms, two legs, two nostrils and a mouth,” our understanding differs: upbringing, education, personal taste, childhood traumas and more all shape how we judge a sound. When I listen to the metal band Arch Enemy, for example, it feels incredibly energizing and satisfying, but for the old lady who lives downstairs it is nothing short of a disaster and an ill omen. Evaluation at this level is therefore highly subjective and the vocabulary very free; different people may use completely different words for the same impression. How would you describe the voice of Stefanie Sun, the Singaporean pop singer? Clear, fresh, natural, moving, warm yet powerful… These descriptions may be a little ambiguous, but there is no denying that they are highly subjective, free and loose.

So when we judge sound by “taste,” we are mostly working at the cognitive level. You can say someone has mediocre taste, but you can’t say they are deaf, because their ears may work perfectly well. Calling them deaf is both unfair and bad form.

PS: The perceptual and cognitive levels both fall within psychoacoustics. At the perceptual level, modern psychoacoustics mainly studies how the path from physical phenomenon to physiological response shapes perception; at the cognitive level, the evaluation dimensions include… (far too many to list; it depends on what you need).

To sum up how the three levels relate:

In fact, the same idea works not only for sound but for anything sensory, such as taste and vision.

Example 1: evaluating a beer

Physical level: alcohol content XX, volume XXX, sugar content XXX, temperature XXX.

Perceptual level: How sour is it? Is it sweet? Is it bitter? Does the fizz have a sharp bite?

Cognitive level: Does it taste good? What occasion is it for?

Example 2: evaluating a painting

Physical level: the RGB value of every pixel.

Perceptual level: Is the picture closer to black-and-white or full of color overall? Is it bright or dark overall?

Cognitive level: René Magritte rocks. Surrealism is such a joy to look at!

How do “evaluation levels” relate to “evaluation perspectives” or “dimensions”?

At the start of this article I used a little exaggeration to paint the delicate relationship between some composers and mixing engineers. In reality, whenever people evaluate or comment on music, or sound in general, they are speaking from a specific “evaluation perspective,” or “evaluation dimension.” Here is how evaluation levels and perspectives relate:

What you think the communication gap between you looks like:

What the gap actually looks like:

Both are talking about how loud and how energetic a sound is, but because they are on different levels, they inevitably talk past each other.

Which level is best? The most badass? I’ll use that one from now on!

That’s the wrong mindset. Each evaluation scenario calls for the level that suits it best. To assess the noise impact of a road on a nearby housing estate, for example, the physical level is the best fit. To assess a voice actor’s expressiveness, the cognitive level is entirely appropriate.

Can every sound be evaluated on all three levels?


Yes. Any sound can be evaluated on the three levels. You can use all of them or only some, depending on your needs and the situation. When judging a singer, for example, we can assess at the physical and perceptual levels whether the pitch (the fundamental frequency) is accurate, and at the cognitive level whether the vowels sound clear and natural.

How do we use this at work?

The core of this methodology is simple: when you speak English to me, I answer in English; when you speak Chinese to me, I answer in Chinese.

The problem described above, talking past each other, is in fact common throughout sound work, and even in visual work. It arises mainly because people are not exchanging their evaluations on the same level, and the result is a great deal of wasted communication. As sound designers in particular, we need enough understanding and practical skill on all three levels to exchange ideas effectively across disciplines and departments, rather than clinging to professional pride, locking ourselves away in an ivory tower and gradually shutting ourselves off.

Now you know why it is so hard for AI to assess the emotion in a voice or to judge timbre, and why its accuracy is so low. Heh heh~

About the author: Zhuoyi Ma holds a master’s degree in acoustics and audio technology from Aalto University in Finland and now works in audio technology research at a game company in Shanghai. Ma is also a member of the Rainbow Chamber Singers, lead singer of the Finnish band Polirytmi, a voice-over director and a phonetics enthusiast.
